topStories.headline: Seventeen AI Cameras Are Watching Hunters Point — and Most Residents Don't Know It
topStories.dek: A new community report maps 17 Flock Safety license-plate readers in Hunters Point as SFPD's citywide AI surveillance network reaches 500 cameras, raising urgent questions about consent, privacy, and who bears the watch.
topStories.body:
A report published October 21 in the San Francisco Bay View puts a neighborhood address on a surveillance network that has grown largely out of public view. According to data from Deflock.org, a crowdsourced national map of automated license-plate readers, 17 Flock Safety ALPR cameras have been counted and mapped in Hunters Point alone. Citywide, SFPD now owns and operates 500 AI-enhanced Flock cameras — a network that began in March 2024 and has expanded year over year.

The technology does considerably more than photograph license plates. Wired reporting cited in a Lawfare analysis published October 6 describes how Flock has built an AI tool that can track vehicles by their patterns of movement alone, identifying potential witnesses based on how frequently their cars pass through a neighborhood, and flagging a driver's associates based on cameras they travel past together. The ACLU describes the combined result as a de facto mass surveillance system: data is uploaded into a nationwide database accessible to any law enforcement agency holding a Flock contract, with limited oversight of how it is used.

Many Bayview–Hunters Point residents appear unaware the cameras are even there. The Bay View piece quotes a woman selling oysters at Third and Palou saying that if she asked ten neighbors, none would know the readers existed. A cashier at a nearby business raised separate concerns about how the data could eventually be used for financial enforcement.

The report arrives amid national pushback. A bipartisan Senate hearing on ALPR privacy took place in September, the ACLU is tracking a growing list of communities that have rejected or canceled Flock contracts, and in San Francisco the Police Commission approved new drone use rules in mid-October — rules that critics said did not go far enough on privacy. Bayview–Hunters Point, which has the city's highest concentration of surveillance cameras relative to its residential footprint, is now squarely in the center of that debate.

topStories.headline: Two Bayview Homicide Suspects Arrested on the Same Morning — One a Juvenile
topStories.dek: SFPD closed two separate fatal shootings from earlier this month with back-to-back announcements on October 20.
topStories.body:
San Francisco police announced two homicide arrests in the Bayview district on the morning of October 20, resolving separate killings that had each occurred in the first half of October.

In the first case, officers responded to the 1100 block of Thomas Avenue around 5:11 p.m. on October 1 and found a man suffering from a gunshot wound. He was hospitalized and later died. Investigators identified 44-year-old San Francisco resident Jorge Alberto Mendoza-Hernandez as the suspect and arrested him on the 600 block of Gilman Avenue in Bayview. He was booked into the county jail on homicide charges. SFPD case number 260-577-378.

In the second case, officers found a man with multiple gunshot wounds on the 1100 block of Wisconsin Street on the evening of October 16. He died at the scene despite paramedics' efforts. Investigators developed probable cause quickly, serving a search warrant on the 1800 block of 25th Street on October 17. There, officers arrested the suspect and seized evidence. The suspect is a juvenile male whose age and name will not be released under state law. He was transported to the Juvenile Justice Center and booked for homicide under California Penal Code 187(a). SFPD case number 260-611-578.

Both investigations remain active and open. Anyone with information on either case is asked to contact SFPD's tip line at 415-575-4444 or submit a tip anonymously through sfpd.org.

topStories.headline: Crocker Amazon Turf Battle Drags Into Fall With No Supervisors Vote Scheduled
topStories.dek: Six months after the Recreation and Park Commission unanimously recommended accepting a $28 million Giants grant, the full Board of Supervisors has not put the Crocker Amazon renovation on its calendar.
topStories.body:
The dispute over Crocker Amazon Park's future is entering its seventh month with no vote in sight at City Hall. The Recreation and Park Commission voted unanimously in April to recommend that the Board of Supervisors accept a $28 million grant from the San Francisco Giants Community Fund for a wholesale renovation of the park's ball diamonds. As of Mission Local's late-September reporting, the Board had not scheduled a hearing, and a round of additional community review had been added before any final action.

The proposed $50 million project — funded equally by the Giants grant and $22 million in city money from the 2020 Health and Recovery bond — would replace natural grass on five of the six renovated ballfields with synthetic turf, install batting cages, improved lighting, a dog play area, and new irrigation. The plan also calls for the removal of roughly 128 mature trees, though Rec & Park has pledged a two-for-one replanting ratio that it says would raise the park's overall tree count from 309 to about 407.

The grassroots group Keep Crocker Real continues to oppose both the synthetic turf and the tree removals, arguing that health and environmental costs outweigh the athletic benefits. Supporters — including youth baseball leagues, the Giants, and Rec & Park — say the deteriorating natural grass fields, routinely closed for weeks at a time due to gopher damage and wet weather, leave young players across the city without enough usable diamonds.

District 11 Supervisor Chyanne Chen, whose district includes the park at Moscow Street and Geneva Avenue, has hosted community meetings but has not taken a public position on the design. Rec & Park lists a potential groundbreaking as early as 2027 or 2028 — contingent on Board approval that has not yet been scheduled.

moreNews.headline: Small Change Arcade Is Open: Pinball, Classic Games, and Community Space at 4740 Mission
moreNews.body: Small Change Arcade, a nonprofit walk-in arcade at 4740 Mission Street in the Excelsior, celebrated its grand opening on October 16 with pinball, classic coin-op cabinet games, live music, and food. Owner Matthew Sengbusch, who has long repaired and rented arcade and pinball machines, now has a public storefront where neighbors can drop in and play. A visitor during Sunday Streets on October 18 reported enthusiastic crowds and said the shop was still buzzing days after opening. The arcade is one of three businesses that received 2026 Storefront Opportunity Grants from the city's Office of Economic and Workforce Development, a program that funds new tenants to open in storefronts that have sat vacant. The other two grant recipients — Mission: Comics–Excelsior at 5196 Mission Street, and City Made Quilts at 1021 Geneva Avenue — opened earlier this year.

moreNews.headline: Bayview's First Pharmacy in Over a Year Is Taking Shape on Third Street, Targeted for Early 2027
moreNews.body: A nonprofit pharmacy called the D10 Community Pharmacy is planned for 5668 Third Street in Bayview — the long-vacant former site of What's the Scoop ice cream parlor — with a projected opening in early 2027, according to an ABC7 report from July 31, 2026. The project is led by Bayview Senior Services' Cathy Davis and Geoffrea Morris, the same team behind the D10 Community Market, a free grocery service for low-income residents that opened in 2024. The pharmacy received a Storefront Opportunity Grant from the city's Office of Economic and Workforce Development. It will sit near three senior housing developments and a T-line stop at Third Street and Paul Avenue. The last Walgreens in Bayview–Hunters Point closed in February 2025, leaving the neighborhood's nearly 35,000 residents without any local pharmacy. A separate Walgreens building at 5300 Third Street was approved in July 2026 by the San Francisco Planning Commission to become an AutoZone — a vote that drew objections from residents who had called for a pharmacy, grocery store, or medical use at the site.
